newsitem.title: USA: New US RFG blends may not be as flexible as hoped.
newsitem.headline: New US RFG blends may not be as flexible as hoped.

text.p: The next generation of cleaner-burning reformulated gasolines may not deliver the flexibility of blending refiners had hoped, an oil executive warned colleagues at an industry conference Monday.

So called "complex model" gasoline, which will be required in the smoggiest U.S. cities from next year, will allow refiners and blenders to meet emissions standards without mandating a specific recipe the way current RFG rules do.
"Unfortunately, this (complex) model is remarkably inflexible," said Bill Cason, a chemical engineer who is now a lawyer at Houston-based firm Mayor Day Caldwell & Keeton LLP.

In what he said was possibly the first major statistical analysis of how the federally-regulated variables in gasoline formulation interact in different blends, Cason stressed problems emerge that have far-reaching economic implications.

"The industry is effectively capped," Cason told executives at the National Petroleum Refiners Association (NPRA) annual meeting, noting the problem will get even worse in the year 2000 when the last scheduled phase of fuel reformulation takes effect.

Cason was referring to how the various fuel parameters refiners can juggle into different recipes, including sulphur, volatility, oxygen, and certain hydrocarbons, will in effect box them in and restrict their blending options.

Specifically, he said his research suggests both sulphur levels and volatility, or Reid vapor pressure (RVP), will have to be pushed to such low levels to achieve emissions target as to render the complex model uneconomical.
"This implies that large reductions in the emissions inventory cannot be achieved solely by changes in motor fuel quality," Cason said.
He said expensively low sulfur levels in the new reformulated gasolines would be the result on focusing so heavily on motor fuels to meet the nitrous oxide emission guidelines.
Removing sulfur from petroleum or petroleum products requires expensive refinery processes, such as hydrotreating.
Cason also said reductions of vapor presure, often achieved by pulling butane out of the fuel, are said to be quite expensive.
Nitrous Oxide, along with volatile organic compounds and searing summer sunlight, is one of the major causes of urban smog.

"If the burden for nitrous oxide is placed on (vehicles), and if the complex model is used as the tool to evaluate the proposed reductions, then sulphur will be forced by the mathematics to be reduced," Cason said.

"The vapor pressure will be limited to approximately 7.0 pounds per square inch...because the equations do not solve for reasonable ranges of physical properties when vapor pressure rises above this level," he added.
